title: The Woman Who Taught Machines to Read

panels.prompt: A Navy office in 1952, a woman in a crisp dark Navy uniform with sharp intelligent eyes and a no-nonsense expression stands confidently before a room of skeptical men in business suits seated around a conference table, behind her a green chalkboard reads 'A PROGRAM THAT TRANSLATES ENGLISH TO MACHINE CODE' in chalk, the men lean back with arms crossed looking doubtful, she stands with one hand on the chalkboard and the other gesturing emphatically, dramatic overhead lighting, tension between skepticism and certainty, comic book style, warm editorial illustration with ink lines and watercolor washes, green #38A169 accent on chalkboard border

panels.text: Grace Brewster Murray Hopper earned her PhD in mathematics from Yale in 1934. In 1943, she joined the Navy and was assigned to program the Harvard Mark I. Her superpower was seeing what was obvious to nobody else: computers would never reach their potential if only mathematicians could program them.

panels.text:
In 1952, Hopper wrote what is widely regarded as the first compiler — a program called A-0 that translated mathematical notation into machine code. "I had a running compiler," she recalled, "and nobody would touch it. They told me a computer could only do arithmetic."

She kept building. A-0 led to A-2, then to FLOW-MATIC (delivered 1958-59), which understood English-like commands: MULTIPLY PRICE BY QUANTITY GIVING TOTAL.

panels.text: The term "bug" for technical faults dates back to Thomas Edison in the 1870s. In 1947, operators working with the Harvard Mark II found an actual moth trapped in a relay. They taped it into the logbook: "First actual case of bug being found." The word "actual" shows they already used "bug" as slang. Hopper loved this story and shared it widely, cementing "debugging" into computing's vocabulary.

A compiler is a program that translates human-readable code into machine code. Hopper's insight was profound: if a computer can manipulate symbols, it can manipulate words just as easily as numbers. The compiler is the bridge between human thought and machine execution — and it's still how most software is built today.

panels.text: Hopper proved computers could understand something beyond raw numbers. But in a different lab, a frustrated mathematician was about to create something even more ambitious — a language that looked like algebra. And IBM was going to bet its reputation on it.
